title: Retell Lecture: mencatat 90 detik, menceritakan ulang 40 detik
title_target: Retell Lecture — notes, key points, and a retelling in your own words
goal: Menceritakan ulang kuliah pendek dalam 40 detik: menangkap topik dan tiga–empat poin utama lewat catatan kata kunci, lalu menyampaikannya dengan kalimat sendiri, tanpa jeda dan tanpa kalimat hafalan kosong.
bekal: mencatat kuliah 90 detik dengan kata kunci, singkatan, dan panah — bukan kalimat
memilih tiga sampai empat poin yang layak diceritakan ulang dan membuang sisanya
menyusun retelling 40 detik: topik → poin → contoh atau akibat → penutup, dengan parafrase

blocks.text: Kamu mendengar potongan kuliah — kadang disertai gambar di layar — sepanjang **sampai 90 detik**, diputar **sekali**. Begitu audio selesai, kamu punya **10 detik** persiapan, lalu nada berbunyi dan mikrofon merekam **40 detik**. Tipe ini muncul kira-kira 2–3 kali, sesudah Describe Image, dan nilainya masuk ke dua skor sekaligus: Listening dan Speaking.

Tiga hal dinilai. **Oral fluency** dan **pronunciation** dinilai mesin, persis seperti di Describe Image. **Content** — seberapa tepat kamu menyampaikan isi kuliah — sejak 7 Agustus 2025 ikut **ditinjau penilai manusia**. Dulu banyak peserta lolos dengan pola *The speaker talked about X. He mentioned Y. He also mentioned Z.* yang hanya menempelkan kata lepas dari catatan. Sekarang orang yang memeriksa jawabanmu mencari satu hal: apakah kamu paham **hubungan** antar-gagasannya.

head: Yang dihargai
Yang dihukum
rows: topik kuliah disebut dengan tepat di kalimat pertama
pembuka hafalan yang cocok untuk kuliah apa pun
tiga–empat poin utama, dengan kata-katamu sendiri
kata lepas yang ditempel tanpa hubungan: *he mentioned sleep, he mentioned memory*
hubungan antar-poin: sebab, akibat, kontras, contoh
menyalin kalimat dosen kata demi kata sampai waktu habis di poin pertama
*In conclusion, the lecture was very informative.*

blocks.title: Tiga hal teknis
items: **Audio hanya sekali.** Tidak ada tombol ulang, dan sesudah *Next* soal tidak bisa dibuka lagi. Catatanmu adalah satu-satunya yang tersisa dari kuliah itu.
**Diam 3 detik = selesai.** Mikrofon berhenti merekam, status berubah jadi *Completed*, dan tidak bisa diulang.
**40 detik ≈ 90–100 kata.** Kuliahnya sendiri 200 kata lebih. Jadi tugasmu memang memilih, dan memilih dengan benar adalah bagian dari nilai content.

blocks.text: Di pusat tes kamu mendapat papan catatan yang bisa dihapus dan sebuah spidol. Selama audio berjalan, tanganmu harus bekerja tanpa membuat telingamu berhenti. Caranya: tulis **sesedikit mungkin, tetapi yang tepat**.

items: **Kata benda, kata kerja kunci, dan angka — bukan kalimat.** Tulis *dark surfaces absorb heat*, bukan *The lecturer says that dark surfaces such as…*
**Satu baris = satu gagasan.** Pindah baris setiap dosen pindah gagasan. Nanti tiap baris menjadi satu kalimat.
**Panah dan simbol untuk hubungan.** Hubungan inilah yang dinilai, jadi harus terlihat di catatanmu.
**Potong kata:** *temp, govt, esp, yrs*. Tidak ada yang membaca catatan ini selain kamu, sepuluh detik kemudian.
**Jangan berhenti mendengar demi mengeja.** Nama yang sulit cukup huruf depannya; saat bicara kamu boleh menyebutnya *the inventor* atau *the researcher*.

blocks.text: Penanda arah: dosen memberitahu kapan harus mencatat

head: Yang diucapkan dosen
Yang kamu lakukan
rows: *Today I'd like to look at… · In this session…*
tulis topiknya di baris paling atas
*The main reason… · A second reason… · On top of that…*
tulis *eg* dan dua–tiga kata; satu contoh sudah cukup
baris baru diawali BUT — kontras hampir selalu poin penting
*As a result… · This means… · The consequences…*
*So… · The key point is… · In other words…*

sections.title: Contoh dibedah: dari audio ke catatan ke jawaban

blocks.text: Baca naskah ini **satu kali** dengan kecepatan orang bicara, sambil mencatat di kertas seperti di tes. Baru sesudah itu bandingkan catatanmu dengan contoh di bawahnya.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Today I'd like to look at a phenomenon known as the urban heat island. Put simply, cities tend to be noticeably warmer than the countryside around them, and the difference is usually greatest at night.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: So why does this happen? The main reason is the materials we build with. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and concrete absorb the sun's energy during the day and release it slowly after sunset. A second reason is the lack of vegetation. Trees provide shade, and they also cool the air as water evaporates from their leaves, so when we replace them with buildings, we lose that natural cooling. On top of that, cars, factories and air conditioners all give off waste heat.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: The consequences are serious. Hotter cities need more electricity for cooling, and during heatwaves the extra warmth increases the risk of illness and death, particularly among elderly people. The good news is that the effect can be reduced. Planting trees, creating green roofs and using lighter, more reflective surfaces have all been shown to bring urban temperatures down. So, the key point is that the way we design our cities largely determines how hot they become.

blocks.title: Catatan di papan
items: UHI = city hotter than countryside, esp night
1) dark surfaces (asphalt, concrete) absorb heat → release at night
2) few trees → no shade, no cooling
3) waste heat: cars, AC
→ more electricity for cooling · heatwave risk, elderly
fix: trees, green roofs, reflective surfaces
! city design decides heat

blocks.text: Tujuh baris tidak muat dalam 40 detik kalau semuanya diceritakan panjang. Dalam 10 detik itu: **nomori urutan bicaramu**, gabungkan baris yang sejenis (tiga penyebab menjadi dua kalimat), dan lingkari baris bertanda ! untuk penutup. Hasilnya empat poin: apa itu *urban heat island* → penyebabnya → akibatnya → cara menguranginya.

blocks.title: Model jawaban (99 kata, ± 38 detik)
items: The lecture was about the urban heat island effect, which means that cities are warmer than the surrounding countryside, especially at night. The lecturer explained that this is mainly caused by dark building materials like asphalt and concrete, which store heat during the day, and by the lack of trees, which normally cool the air. Waste heat from cars and air conditioners makes it worse. As a result, cities use more energy for cooling, and heatwaves become more dangerous for older people. He concluded that planting trees and using reflective surfaces can reduce the problem, so city design matters.

head: Kata dosen
Kata kamu
Tekniknya
rows: *noticeably warmer than the countryside around them*
frasa diringkas jadi satu kata sifat
*absorb the sun's energy during the day*
kata umum diganti kata yang lebih mudah diucapkan
*increases the risk of illness and death, particularly among elderly people*
*heatwaves become more dangerous for older people*
kata benda diubah jadi kata sifat

blocks.text: Istilah intinya — *urban heat island, asphalt, concrete* — **tidak** diparafrase. Kata teknis justru harus muncul karena itulah isi kuliahnya; yang diubah adalah kalimat di sekelilingnya.

sections.title: Kerangka menceritakan ulang — dan kalau kamu ketinggalan

blocks.title: Empat langkah, 40 detik
items: **1. Topik (± 6 detik)** — *The lecture was about…* disusul topik yang tepat, kalau bisa dengan definisinya. Bukan *about a topic*, bukan *about science*.
**2. Poin utama (± 20 detik)** — dua–tiga poin dari catatan, disambung kata hubung yang menunjukkan hubungannya: *because, which means, in contrast, as a result*.
**3. Contoh atau akibat (± 8 detik)** — satu saja: eksperimen, angka, atau akibat yang disebut dosen.
**4. Penutup (± 6 detik)** — kesimpulan dosen (baris bertanda ! di catatanmu), bukan penilaianmu tentang kuliahnya: *He concluded that… · So… · Overall,…*

blocks.text: Urutan ini yang dihafal; kalimatnya tidak. Sesudah kalimat pertama, langsung sampaikan isinya: *Dark materials store heat*, bukan *He said that… He said that… He said that…* Kata kerja pelapor cukup dua–tiga kali dan boleh bervariasi: *explained, pointed out, warned, concluded*. Pakai **past tense** untuk melaporkan (*the lecturer explained*) dan **present tense** untuk fakta umum (*cities are warmer*).

blocks.title: Kalau kamu ketinggalan
items: **Kehilangan satu bagian?** Lepaskan. Mengejar kalimat yang sudah lewat membuatmu kehilangan kalimat yang sedang diucapkan. Dua poin yang jelas hubungannya lebih baik daripada empat poin kabur.
**Hanya dapat topik dan beberapa kata?** Susun kalimat yang jujur dari kata-kata itu. Jangan mengarang fakta yang tidak diucapkan dosen: penilai manusia membandingkan jawabanmu dengan isi kuliahnya.
**Ada gambar di layar?** Judul dan labelnya adalah catatan gratis — topik dan kata kunci sudah tertulis di situ.
**Buntu saat bicara?** Jangan diam dan jangan meralat. Lompat ke baris berikutnya di catatan, atau langsung ke penutup.
**Selesai di detik ke-30?** Tidak apa-apa. Jangan mengisi sisa waktu dengan mengulang poin; pengulangan merusak fluency.

blocks.text: Putar audionya dulu dan kerjakan latihan TANPA membaca naskah di bawah; naskah ini untuk memeriksa sesudahnya.

Urutan kerja untuk tiap kuliah: dengarkan **sekali** sambil mencatat → 10 detik menomori catatan → rekam retelling-mu 40 detik di ponsel. Sesudah empat kuliah dan empat rekaman selesai, kerjakan Latihan dari catatanmu.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: In this session I want to consider why the printing press is often described as one of the most important inventions in history. Around 1450, in the German city of Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg developed a press that used movable metal type. Each letter was a separate piece of metal, so the letters could be arranged into a page, printed many times, and then reused.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Before this, books in Europe were copied by hand, usually by monks. A single copy of a long book could take months to produce, which meant that books were extremely expensive and were owned mostly by the Church and the very rich. Printing changed that. A press could turn out hundreds of identical copies in the time a scribe needed for one, and so the price of books fell dramatically.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: The effects went far beyond cheaper books. As books became affordable, more people had a reason to learn to read, and literacy slowly spread. New ideas also travelled faster. Religious reformers and, later, scientists could share their work with thousands of readers across Europe, and because every copy was the same, scholars in different countries could discuss exactly the same text. So printing didn't just copy knowledge; it changed who had access to it.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.text: Let's turn to a question that matters to every student: what does sleep actually do for memory? For a long time, sleep was seen as a passive state, a period when the brain simply switched off. We now know that this is wrong. While you sleep, your brain is busy processing what you learned during the day.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.text: The key process is called consolidation. New memories are first held in a region called the hippocampus, which works rather like a temporary store. During deep sleep, the brain replays these recent experiences and gradually transfers them to the cortex, where they are kept for the long term. In other words, sleep turns fragile, short-term memories into stable ones.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.text: The evidence for this is strong. In a typical experiment, two groups learn the same list of words. One group then sleeps, while the other stays awake for the same number of hours. When they are tested, the group that slept consistently remembers more. This has a very practical implication. Staying up all night before an exam may feel productive, but it deprives the brain of the time it needs to store information. So if you want to remember what you study, sleep is not a luxury; it is part of the learning process.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Today's topic is coral bleaching, and to understand it we first need to understand how a healthy coral lives. Corals are animals, but they depend on tiny algae that live inside their tissues. The relationship benefits both sides. The algae get a safe place to live, and in return they produce food through photosynthesis, supplying most of the energy the coral needs. They also give the coral its colour.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: The problem begins when the sea becomes too warm. If the water temperature stays just one or two degrees above the normal summer maximum for several weeks, the coral becomes stressed and expels its algae. Without them, the coral's white skeleton shows through its transparent tissue, which is why we call it bleaching.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Now, a bleached coral is not dead. If the water cools quickly enough, the algae can return and the coral recovers. But if the heat continues, the coral slowly starves. This matters far beyond the reef itself. Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they support roughly a quarter of all marine species, and millions of people rely on them for food and for protection from storms. As the oceans warm, bleaching events are becoming more frequent, leaving reefs less time to recover between them.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.text: I'd like to begin today with a very old example that economists still use: Adam Smith's pin factory. In his book The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, Smith described a small workshop where pins were made. He pointed out that one worker, doing every step alone, could make no more than twenty pins in a day. But when the work was divided into about eighteen separate tasks, with each worker doing only one or two of them, ten workers together could produce around forty-eight thousand pins a day.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.text: Smith called this the division of labour, and he gave several reasons why it raises output so sharply. Workers become faster and more skilled when they repeat a single task. They don't lose time moving from one job to another. And when a task is simple, it is easier to invent a machine to do it.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.text: However, Smith also saw a cost. He warned that people who spend their whole lives performing a few simple operations have no opportunity to use their minds, and that this could damage their intelligence and well-being. That tension is still with us. Specialisation makes modern economies enormously productive, but it can also make work repetitive and unsatisfying, which is why many companies now rotate staff between tasks.

blocks.text: Sesudah Latihan selesai, buka naskah di atas dan dengarkan keempat rekamanmu dengan telinga penilai. Lalu bandingkan dengan model di bagian *Pembahasan* — yang dicocokkan adalah poin yang dipilih, bukan kalimatnya.

blocks.title: Daftar periksa
items: **Topik** — apakah kalimat pertamamu menyebut topik yang tepat, bukan hanya bidangnya?
**Poin** — hitung poinmu yang juga ada di naskah. Tiga atau empat? Adakah yang kamu karang?
**Hubungan** — tandai setiap *because, so, however, as a result*. Kalau tidak ada satu pun, jawabanmu masih berupa daftar.
**Kata sendiri** — adakah tujuh kata berturut-turut yang sama persis dengan naskah? Parafrasekan bagian itu.
**Irama** — jeda panjang, pengulangan, ralat: targetnya nol, dan selesai sebelum detik ke-40.

blocks.text: Untuk skor mesin yang sebenarnya, pakai tes latihan resmi berskor dari Pearson. Kalau kamu ingin catatan dan rekamanmu dibedah satu per satu, itu yang dikerjakan di kelas Private PTE Linguo.

Jawaban
Alasan & pengecoh
rows: *the price of books fell dramatically* dan penutupnya *it changed who had access to it*. (A) memakai kata *monks*, padahal mereka penyalin tangan sebelum mesin cetak; (C) masuk akal tetapi tidak disebut; (D) bertentangan dengan *the effects went far beyond*.

*the brain replays these recent experiences and gradually transfers them to the cortex*. (A) justru pandangan lama yang dibantah (*this is wrong*); (B) hippocampus hanya *a temporary store*; (C) mimpi tidak disebut.
*expels its algae* dan *leaving reefs less time to recover*. (B) bertentangan dengan *a bleached coral is not dead*; (C) polusi tidak disebut; (D) alga dikeluarkan, bukan tumbuh terlalu cepat.

*ten workers together could produce around forty-eight thousand pins*, lalu *However, Smith also saw a cost*. (A) mesin hanya salah satu dari tiga alasan; (B) upah tidak disebut; (D) kebalikan dari isi kuliah.
Topik, mekanisme dengan panah, satu contoh, dan implikasinya. (A) menyalin kalimat pembuka dan terputus; (B) kata lepas tanpa hubungan, hanya cukup untuk jawaban *he mentioned…*
Contoh, angka yang terikat pada artinya, tiga alasan, dan kontras BUT. (B) kalimat tentang Smith, bukan isi kuliah; (C) lima angka tanpa keterangan tidak bisa diceritakan ulang.
Susunan sebelum–sesudah dengan panah akibat. (A) kata lepas; (C) salinan kalimat pembuka.
*they depend on tiny algae that live inside their tissues*.
*the coral becomes stressed and expels its algae*. *absorb* (menyerap) berlawanan artinya.
*If the water cools quickly enough, the algae can return and the coral recovers*.
*if the heat continues, the coral slowly starves* — alga adalah sumber sebagian besar energinya.
*they support roughly a quarter of all marine species*. *half* tidak disebut.
*Each letter was a separate piece of metal… and then reused*.
Benar di dunia nyata, tetapi dosen hanya membahas Eropa. Di retelling, pengetahuan dari luar audio tidak menambah nilai content.
*the group that slept consistently remembers more*.
*millions of people rely on them for food and for protection from storms*.
Upah tidak dibahas sama sekali; yang naik adalah jumlah produksi (*output*).
Satu kalimat (B) memuat hubungan sebab-akibat yang lengkap. (A) adalah template kata lepas yang kini dihukum pada content.
Isi keduanya mirip, tetapi (B) penuh pengulangan, pengisi, dan ralat (*sorry*), yang dihitung mesin sebagai gangguan fluency.
Separuh kuliah yang diceritakan dengan jelas tetap mendapat nilai content. Karangan sendiri (A) tidak ada di audio dan terbaca oleh penilai manusia.

blocks.title: Lecture 1 · The printing press
items: The lecture was about the printing press and why it was such an important invention. The lecturer explained that around 1450 Gutenberg built a press with movable metal type, so pages could be printed many times. Before that, books were copied by hand, which took months and made them very expensive. Printing produced hundreds of copies quickly, so prices fell sharply. As a result, more people learned to read, and new religious and scientific ideas spread across Europe. Overall, printing changed who had access to knowledge.

blocks.title: Lecture 2 · Sleep and memory
items: The professor discussed how sleep helps memory. She said that sleep is not a passive state, because the brain keeps working on what we learned during the day. New memories are first stored in the hippocampus, and during deep sleep they are replayed and moved to the cortex for long-term storage. Experiments support this: people who sleep after learning a word list remember more than people who stay awake. Therefore, studying all night before an exam is a bad idea, and sleep should be seen as part of learning.

blocks.title: Lecture 3 · Coral bleaching
items: The lecture explained that corals depend on tiny algae, which live inside them and supply most of their energy. When the sea stays too warm for several weeks, corals become stressed and expel the algae, so they turn white. A bleached coral is still alive and can recover if the water cools quickly. If the heat continues, however, the coral slowly starves. This is serious because reefs support about a quarter of all marine species. Overall, warmer oceans mean more frequent bleaching and less time for reefs to recover.

blocks.title: Lecture 4 · The division of labour
items: The professor talked about the division of labour, using Adam Smith's example of a pin factory. One worker alone could make only about twenty pins a day, but ten workers who divided the job into small tasks could make around forty-eight thousand. This is because people get faster at one task and waste no time changing jobs, and simple tasks are easier to give to machines. However, Smith warned that repetitive work can harm workers' minds. So specialisation raises productivity, but it can also make work dull.

blocks.title: Yang perlu dicatat
items: Keempat model berjalan di urutan yang sama — topik, poin, contoh atau akibat, penutup — tetapi tiap kalimatnya hanya cocok untuk kuliahnya sendiri. Kerangka dihafal, isi tidak.
Setiap model memuat minimal tiga kata hubung (*so, because, as a result, however, therefore*). Itulah yang membedakan retelling dari daftar kata, dan itulah yang dicari penilai manusia.
Angka dipakai seperlunya: 1450; twenty dan forty-eight thousand; a quarter. Angka yang tidak kamu yakini lebih baik diganti kata (*a small share, far more*) daripada salah sebut.
